passage: In the kasba, everybody knew everybody, so when Kavitha posted a video mocking the new maths teacher's accent, it was round the whole school by lunch. She deleted it that evening. Her cousin Sunaina, home from college, showed her a screenshot on her own phone. "Someone saved it. It's in four groups already." Kavitha's stomach dropped. "But I deleted it." "Deleting only removes your copy," Sunaina said gently. The next week, the teacher was quieter in class, and Kavitha couldn't look at her. Her father, who ran the photocopy shop, had heard about it from a customer. Kavitha went to the teacher after school and apologised, her voice shaking. She didn't know if the teacher forgave her. She stopped posting for a while.

qa.q: How many groups had Kavitha's video reached according to Sunaina?
qa.a: It had reached four groups already.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha's stomach drop when she saw the screenshot?
qa.a: She realised deleting the video had not erased it, and that her joke was now out of her control and hurting the teacher and her own name.

qa.q: What was wise about Kavitha's response after she learned the video had spread?
qa.a: She apologised to the teacher in person instead of hiding, which took responsibility even though she could not undo the posts.

qa.q: How might the maths teacher feel after the video spread?
qa.a: She was likely hurt and self-conscious, since she became quieter in class, and she may take time to trust the students again.

grounding: It shows a teen learning that a deleted post had already been saved and shared, affecting her reputation and another person.

passage: Oskar was sixteen and applying for a summer job at the café near his flat in Gothenburg. The owner, a friendly woman with flour on her sleeves, said, "I looked you up, of course." Oskar went pale. His friend Xin was waiting outside, and after the interview Oskar grabbed her arm. "What did she see?" They searched his name together. The first things: a school football photo, a comment he'd written at thirteen calling a referee an idiot, and a silly video of him falling off a bench. "The comment's the worst," Xin said. Oskar winced. "I was thirteen!" "It doesn't say that on it." That night he went through his old accounts, removing what he could and making others private. He still got the job.

qa.q: Where was the café Oskar applied to?
qa.a: It was near his flat in Gothenburg.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling when the owner said she had looked him up?
qa.a: He was suddenly worried and embarrassed, afraid she had seen old posts he no longer wanted linked to him.

qa.q: What could Oskar do from now on to protect his online reputation?
qa.a: He could pause before posting and ask whether he'd be fine with a future employer or teacher seeing it.

qa.q: How does Xin see Oskar's old comment?
qa.a: She sees it as the worst item because, without his age attached, it looks like the current Oskar being rude, not a younger boy.

grounding: It shows a teen discovering that old comments and photos persist online and shape how others see him.

passage: The school's computer lab had a poster that said "Think before you post," and nobody read it. Then, during the careers fair, a college recruiter showed the Class 11 students a slide of anonymous posts from applicants: a rude joke, a photo mocking a classmate, a fight in a comment section. "These are real," he said. "Some were years old." Hansa glanced at Rafiq. He had shared a meme about a girl in their class last month. Rafiq stared at his shoes. After the session, he pulled out his phone in the corridor. "Help me find it," he muttered. They found the meme had been shared by eleven other people. He deleted his, then messaged the girl to say sorry. Hansa noticed his hands shaking as he typed.

qa.q: How many other people had shared Rafiq's meme?
qa.a: Eleven other people had shared it.

qa.q: What does Rafiq staring at his shoes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed and uneasy, because the recruiter's slides reminded him of the meme he had shared about a classmate.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on the recruiter's talk for students like Rafiq?
qa.a: The teacher could give time to review their own accounts and discuss how to repair harm, like apologising, not just deleting.

qa.q: How might the girl in the meme feel when she gets Rafiq's apology?
qa.a: She might feel relieved that he admitted it, though still hurt that the meme had spread so widely.

grounding: It shows teens realising that posts spread and persist and can affect future chances and other people.

passage:
Dear Tanvir,
Maasi said you just started posting, so big-sister-cousin advice, whether you want it or not.
Last month I applied for the student editor post at college. In the interview, the teacher said, 'We had a look at your public profile.' My stomach dropped. At thirteen, I'd left a nasty comment under a classmate's dance video. I'd forgotten it. They hadn't. I explained, apologised, said I'd changed. I still got the post, but I felt about six inches tall.
So, three things. Before you post, ask: would I be fine with a teacher, a future boss or Nani seeing this? Screenshots last forever, even after you delete. And be the kind of person online you are at dinner.
Love,
Sudha didi

qa.q: What had Sudha done at thirteen that came up in her interview?
qa.a: She had left a nasty comment under a classmate's dance video.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when the teacher mentioned her public profile?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped and she felt ashamed, about six inches tall, even though she had changed.

qa.q: Which of Sudha's tips would help Tanvir most before posting?
qa.a: Asking whether Tanvir would be fine with a teacher, future boss or Nani seeing it, since posts and screenshots can last.

qa.q: How might the classmate from the dance video feel if they knew about that comment years later?
qa.a: They might still remember the hurt, showing that online comments can affect people long after they're written.

grounding: A teen writes to her cousin about how old posts and comments persist and shape reputation.

passage: Okay Nirmala, you asked why I'm so careful now. So, last year, at Diwali, I snapped a photo of Harpreet mid-sneeze with laddoo crumbs everywhere. Honestly hilarious. I posted it with a caption and it got loads of likes. Harpreet asked me to delete it that night and I did, straight away. I thought that was the end. Two months later, it turned up as a sticker in the class group. Someone had screenshotted it. People sent it every time he spoke. He stopped talking in the group. And the worst part? Everyone knew I'd started it. I apologised properly, face to face. Now I've got a rule: if it's someone else's face, I ask. If it's mine, I think twice.

qa.q: How did Harpreet seem to feel when the sticker kept being sent?

qa.q: Why is the narrator's new rule a sensible one?

passage:
I'm Rehana, Eshaan's older sister. Last month, Eshaan, sixteen, posted a meme mocking his maths teacher's accent on his class group. Everyone laughed. He deleted it an hour later when he started to feel bad.
But someone had already taken a screenshot. By the next morning, it was on three other groups, and a parent had forwarded it to the principal.
I watched my brother sit on the stairs with his head in his hands. He said, “I deleted it. Why is it still there?”
He wrote a real apology to the teacher, in person, not online. The teacher accepted it, but said, “Remember, the internet doesn't forget.”
Now Eshaan reads every post twice before sending. Sometimes he doesn't send at all.

qa.q: Who forwarded the meme to the principal?
qa.a: A parent had forwarded it to the principal.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when he realised the meme was still circulating?
qa.a: He felt shocked and ashamed, sitting with his head in his hands.

qa.q: What did Eshaan do to repair the harm, and what habit did he learn?
qa.a: He apologised to the teacher in person, and now he reads every post twice before sending.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt seeing the meme?
qa.a: The teacher was probably hurt and embarrassed by the mockery.

grounding: An older sister observes her brother learn that a deleted post can persist and shape reputation.

passage:
Before: On a Saturday in April, Baljeet, seventeen, posted a photo from a party with a caption mocking his friend Parul's dancing. Fifty likes. Parul didn't reply.
During: Three weeks later, a senior from their school told everyone he'd lost a summer internship because the company found his old, rude comments online. Baljeet felt his stomach tighten.
After: That weekend, he scrolled back through his own profile for two hours. He deleted the Parul post and messaged her: “That was mean. Sorry.” He made his account private and wrote a rule on a sticky note by his desk: Would I say this with my grandmother watching?
Parul replied: “Took you long enough. Thanks.”

qa.q: What rule did Baljeet write on a sticky note?
qa.a: Would I say this with my grandmother watching?

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when he heard about the senior's lost internship?
qa.a: He felt worried and uneasy, his stomach tightening.

qa.q: What steps did Baljeet take to protect his reputation and repair harm?
qa.a: He deleted the mean post, apologised to Parul, made his account private and set a rule for future posts.

qa.q: How did Parul react to Baljeet's apology?
qa.a: She accepted it, saying it took long enough but thanking him.

grounding: Over a few weeks a seventeen-year-old realises posts persist and repairs his online footprint.

passage:
Lakshmi, you want to post that video of your friend falling? Wait. Let your Aadhya Masi tell you something.
When I was fifteen, I wrote nasty comments on a music forum. I thought I was funny and nobody knew my real name. I used the same username everywhere.
Ten years later, I applied for a job at a design studio. In the interview, the manager smiled and said, “Is this you?” and showed me one of my old comments. It was cruel. I went red to my ears.
I told the truth. I said I was fifteen and ashamed of it. I got the job, but only because I didn't lie.
That night I deleted everything I could find. Some I couldn't. They're still out there, Lakshmi.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when the manager showed the old comment?

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Aadhya get the job, and why?
qa.a: Telling the truth about the comment and admitting she was ashamed, which showed honesty and growth.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen young Aadhya's cruel comment?
qa.a: The manager probably found it worrying, but was impressed by her honesty in the interview.

passage:
Ritu's scholarship interview was in two hours, and the panel had asked for her social media handles.
She scrolled back through her old posts in a panic. Most were fine. Then she found it: a comment from two years ago, under Ujjwal's post, mocking a classmate's accent. It had forty laughing reactions.
Ritu deleted it. Then Ujjwal texted: "Someone screenshotted that old thread. It's in a group chat."
Her stomach sank. Deleting didn't erase it.
In the interview, the panel didn't mention it. But on the way home, Ritu messaged the classmate: "I wrote something mean about you two years ago. I'm sorry. It was wrong."
The classmate replied: "Thanks for saying it."
Ritu spent the evening going through every old post.

passage:
After the Holi party in their Bengaluru colony, Leela scrolled through her photos. One showed Mahima mid-laugh, mouth open, face covered in green, hair everywhere.
"This is hilarious," said Leela. "I'm posting it."
Mahima grabbed her wrist. "Please don't. That picture will be there forever. My cousin is applying to colleges and they check everything. Someone could tag me."
"It's just a funny photo."
"Funny to you. But I didn't say yes."
Leela looked at the photo again. She thought of how she'd feel if it were her.
"Okay. What about this one?" It was both of them, colourful but smiling.
Mahima nodded. "That one's fine."
Leela posted it, and deleted the other.

qa.q: What colour was Mahima's face in the photo?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she grabbed Leela's wrist?
qa.a: Mahima felt anxious and embarrassed at the idea of an unflattering photo being online forever.

qa.q: What did Leela do well once Mahima objected?
qa.a: She listened, imagined how she'd feel, offered a photo they both liked and deleted the other.

qa.q: What would change if Leela had posted the first photo anyway?
qa.a: Mahima could feel betrayed and exposed, and the unflattering picture might stay online and be tagged or shared long after the party.

grounding: A teen asks a friend not to post an embarrassing photo, since posts persist and shape reputation.

passage:
"Have you seen this?" Simran held out her phone. It was a video of Siddharth from Class 8, pretending to be a teacher with a fake accent.
Siddharth went pale. "Where did that come from? I deleted it."
"Someone saved it. It's going round the Class 11 group."
"But that was three years ago. I was stupid."
"People don't know that. They just see it now."
Siddharth put his head in his hands. "The teacher I was copying is still here."
Simran sat down. "Then maybe say sorry to her first, before she sees it from someone else."
Siddharth was silent for a long time. Then he stood up. "Okay. Come with me?"
"I'll wait outside the staff room."

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he put his head in his hands?
qa.a: Siddharth felt ashamed and worried about how the teacher would see it.

qa.a: She suggested apologising to the teacher before she saw it from others, which shows responsibility and respect.

qa.q: How might the teacher feel if Siddharth apologises before she sees the video?
qa.a: The teacher might still be hurt, but she'd likely respect him for coming to her first.

grounding: A teen faces an old mocking video that resurfaced and decides to apologise.

passage:
When I was thirteen I posted a meme about our maths teacher's handwriting. Just a photo of the board with a joke caption. Forty people laughed at it. I felt clever.
I deleted it a week later, when I got bored of it. I thought that was the end.
Two years later I stood for class prefect. The evening before the vote, Jyoti forwarded me a screenshot. Someone had saved it. It was going round the class group with "Is THIS our prefect?"
My stomach dropped. I couldn't delete a screenshot.
So I didn't try to hide. I went to Sir and apologised, properly. Then, in my speech, I said, "Some of you have seen my old post. It was unkind and I'm sorry. I'm Bidisha, and I'm not that person now."
I lost by six votes. But Sir smiles at me now.

qa.q: What did the class group caption on the screenshot say?
qa.a: "Is THIS our prefect?"

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when Jyoti forwarded the screenshot?
qa.a: Bidisha felt shocked and ashamed, and the passage says Bidisha's stomach dropped.

qa.q: What went right in how Bidisha handled the old post, and what could have prevented it?
qa.a: Owning it and apologising to Sir and the class was honest; thinking before posting about a real person would have prevented it.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when Bidisha came to apologise?
qa.a: Sir may have felt hurt by the old joke but touched and respected that Bidisha came to say sorry directly.

grounding: Shows a teen discovering that a deleted post persisted and shaped reputation years later.

passage:
Counsellor's note, 15 November. Binita (school counsellor).
Anirban came to me worried. He has a state football trial next month and a friend told him selectors "check your profile". He was scrolling through three years of posts, deleting in a panic.
We went through them together, calmly. Most were fine: matches, his dog. A few needed thought: a video of him and friends mocking another team, a comment calling a referee "blind". He went red reading those. He said, "I didn't think anyone would ever see it again."
We talked about what the posts say about him to a stranger. He deleted the mocking video, and he messaged the other team's captain to apologise. The comment was on someone else's page; he asked them to remove it.
Plan: he'll think "Would I say this to their face?" before posting. I'll check in after the trial.

qa.q: What did a friend tell Anirban about the selectors?
qa.a: A friend told him selectors "check your profile".

qa.q: Why did Anirban go red reading the video and the referee comment?
qa.a: Anirban felt embarrassed and ashamed, because he hadn't expected those posts to be seen again, and they showed him mocking people.

qa.q: What would you advise a teen in Anirban's place?
qa.a: Review posts calmly, remove what is unkind, apologise where someone was hurt, and think "Would I say this to their face?" before posting.

qa.q: How might the other team's captain see Anirban's apology?
qa.a: The captain might be surprised and feel respected, seeing that the mocking was taken seriously even years later.

grounding: Illustrates a counsellor helping a teen see that old posts persist and shape how strangers judge him.

Saturday night
Diary, Saurabh here. Arohi's birthday party was fun until she said, "Post the group pic!"
In the best photo, Ved is mid-sneeze. Honestly it's hilarious. Everyone wanted it up. But I kept thinking: in a year, someone will screenshot it and make stickers, like they did to Priyanshu last year. Ved still gets called "Tomato Face" from that.
So I texted Ved: "Can I post the sneeze one?" He wrote back, "PLEASE don't."
Arohi was annoyed. "You're so serious." We posted the other one where everyone's normal. Nobody died.
Later Ved sent me a thank-you meme, privately. It's weird how one photo can follow you around. I think I'm going to go through my own old posts this weekend.

qa.a: Saurabh felt uneasy and worried that it could be screenshotted and follow Ved around, like Priyanshu's photo did.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Ved before posting worked, because the person in the photo got to decide about their own image.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Saurabh's choice later?
qa.a: Arohi was annoyed at the party, but later she might see that Saurabh protected a friend without spoiling her birthday.

grounding: Shows a teen thinking about how a photo persists and could shape a friend's reputation, and asking consent before posting.
